```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(effectzones)
library(ggplot2)
```

effectzones draws a background behind estimates and confidence intervals.
The background marks regions of the effect axis that someone has judged
"small", "large", "clinically trivial" or "beneficial". The package never
looks at your estimates: it does not test them, classify them or compute
any probability. You read the interval against the background, and you
decide what it means.

## Why backgrounds instead of verdicts

A confidence interval already contains the inferential information: the
range of effects compatible with the data under the model. What readers
often lack is a reference frame for magnitude. Is a difference of 0.5 kg
large? Is an odds ratio of 1.4 worth acting on? Benchmarks answer that
question, imperfectly, and putting them behind the interval shows the
interval and the benchmark together without merging them into a verdict.

A verdict ("likely beneficial", "trivial") hides two things: where the
interval lies relative to the threshold, and how arbitrary the threshold
is. A background shows both. An interval that straddles a boundary is
visibly ambiguous; a soft, fading boundary is visibly a convention, not a
natural discontinuity.

The basic plot, a Tukey post-hoc comparison over effect-size zones:

```{r tukey-es}
fit <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
plot_contrasts(
  fit,
  zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), labels = TRUE)
)
```

Two layers do the work, and you can use them in any ggplot:

* `geom_es_zones()`: effect-size magnitude zones around the null.
* `geom_mcid_zones()`: harm / trivial / benefit zones from a minimal
  clinically important difference (MCID).

Add the zones layer **first**, so that points, error bars and reference
lines are drawn on top of it. By default the zones do not change the axis
limits: they fill whatever range your data define, and the outermost zones
extend to the panel edges. The legend lists only the zones that appear in
the plot. Use `expand = TRUE` if every cut-point should be visible.

## Choosing a benchmark set, and why there is no default

`geom_es_zones()` has no default thresholds. Calling it without them is an
error that lists the published sets:

```{r no-default, error = TRUE}
geom_es_zones()
```

This is deliberate. Cohen (1988) proposed d = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 as
conventions to fall back on when nothing better is known about the area of
research, and warned against using them mechanically. Later sets were
derived from what is typical in particular literatures: Gignac & Szodorai
(2016) from meta-analytic correlations in individual-differences research,
Funder & Ozer (2019) from a broader argument about psychological effects.
A "medium" effect in one field is large in another. Choosing the set is a
substantive decision, and the plot should record it: the legend title
names the source.

```{r benchmarks}
es_benchmarks()
```

If your field has its own thresholds, use them:

```{r custom}
my_cuts <- es_thresholds(
  cuts = c(0.1, 0.3),
  labels = c("trivial", "modest", "substantial"),
  metric = "d",
  source = "Protocol v2, section 9"
)
my_cuts
```

The cited sources define cut-points. The label of the innermost zone
("negligible") is a convention of this package, not of the sources. Rename
any zone with `zone_labels`, either all at once or by name:

```{r rename, fig.height = 2.6}
plot_contrasts(
  fit,
  zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"),
                        zone_labels = c(negligible = "below small"))
)
```

## Converting thresholds to the plot scale, and which SD to use

Benchmarks are usually standardised; estimates are often not. Contrasts
from an ANOVA are differences in the outcome's own units, so standardised
thresholds have to be converted: a cut d is drawn at d × SD.

```{r convert}
to_plot_scale(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), sd = 2)
```

Which SD to use is not a technicality: the same benchmark drawn with a
different SD lands in a different place, and changes how the intervals
read.

**One-way models.** In `aov(y ~ group)` the residual SD (the square root of
the ANOVA's mean squared error) is the pooled within-group SD. That is the
usual denominator of Cohen's d, and it is the same quantity the ANOVA F
test and the Tukey intervals already rely on, under the same equal-variance
assumption. `plot_contrasts()` therefore takes it from the model
automatically and prints its value. It works from the `aov` fit, from an
`emmeans()` grid of means, and from a `TukeyHSD` object: `TukeyHSD()` keeps
the call that fitted the model but not the model itself, so the call is
re-run and the result is used only if it reproduces the Tukey contrasts
exactly.

```{r tukey-object, fig.height = 2.6}
tk <- TukeyHSD(fit)
plot_contrasts(tk, zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d")))
```

**Everything else.** With several factors, covariates or interactions, the
residual SD is what is left after removing the other effects. A d built on
it is a *partial* standardised difference, larger than the d you would get
from the raw within-group SD, and whether your benchmarks meant that is a
substantive question. In that case `plot_contrasts()` does not choose: it
stops and asks for `sd`. You can accept the residual SD explicitly with
`sd = pooled_sd(model)`, or give the SD your benchmarks refer to:

```{r two-way, error = TRUE, fig.height = 2.6}
fit2 <- aov(breaks ~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks)
plot_contrasts(fit2, which = "tension",
               zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d")))

plot_contrasts(fit2, which = "tension",
               zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"),
                                     sd = pooled_sd(fit2)))
```

Other SDs can be the better choice: a **baseline or reference-population
SD** when the benchmark was defined relative to it, or when the treatment
changes the variance. In models with several variance components (repeated
measures, random effects) there is no single SD; supply the one your
benchmark refers to.

For **ratios** (odds ratios, risk ratios), a cut c is drawn at c and 1/c,
symmetric on the log scale, unless the thresholds say otherwise (below).
Use `scale = "log"`, `null = 1`, and a log axis:

```{r or}
or <- data.frame(
  term = c("Exposure A", "Exposure B", "Exposure C", "Exposure D"),
  estimate = c(0.72, 1.45, 2.60, 5.10),
  lower = c(0.48, 1.02, 1.55, 2.30),
  upper = c(1.08, 2.06, 4.36, 11.3)
)
ggplot(or, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("chen_or"), scale = "log", null = 1,
                labels = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (95% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Chen, Cohen & Chen (2010) derived these odds ratios as the equivalents of
d = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 **when the event rate in the reference group is 1%**.
Their method places both groups on a latent normal scale: with reference
risk p0, a shift d gives an exposed risk p1 = Φ(Φ⁻¹(p0) + d), and the odds
ratio follows from p0 and p1. `chen_or_thresholds()` implements it for any
baseline risk; it reproduces the published 1% values (1.68, 3.47, 6.71) and
5% values (1.52, 2.74, 4.72):

```{r chen}
chen_or_thresholds(0.10)
```

The same model shows that the zones are **not symmetric**. A protective
shift of −d does not give 1/OR: at a 1% baseline, d = −0.8 corresponds to
OR = 1/11.4, not 1/6.71. The two sides agree only at a 50% baseline. So
both `es_benchmarks("chen_or")` and `chen_or_thresholds()` draw the
boundaries below 1 from negative d. Chen et al. published only the values
above 1; the ones below 1 apply their method and are labelled as such.
Make sure the baseline risk is the risk in the reference group of *your*
odds ratios (the denominator group).

Alternatively, standardised thresholds can be converted to odds ratios with
the approximation log(OR) = d × π / √3 (Chinn 2000), which assumes a
logistic latent variable. Note that it gives different cut-points from
Chen et al.:

```{r chinn}
to_plot_scale(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), scale = "log")$cuts
```

Correlations, η² and Cohen's f are drawn on their own scale only; there is
no conversion from them to raw differences.

## Anchor-based and distribution-based MCIDs

The MCID was introduced as "the smallest difference in score in the domain
of interest which patients perceive as beneficial" (Jaeschke, Singer &
Guyatt 1989). It is a statement about patients, so the preferred way to
estimate it is **anchor-based**: relate score changes to an external
judgement such as a global rating of change.

**Distribution-based** values (half an SD, one standard error of
measurement) describe the spread or the measurement error of the score,
not what patients value. McGlothlin & Lewis (2014) point out that such
values are not patient-derived. effectzones never computes an MCID for you;
if you want a distribution-based value you have to ask for one, and the
legend marks it provisional:

```{r provisional}
prov <- mcid_distribution(sd = 0.7, method = "half_sd")
prov
plot_contrasts(TukeyHSD(fit), zones = geom_mcid_zones(prov))
```

Norman, Sloan & Wyrwich (2003) observed that many anchor-based MCIDs for
health-related quality of life are close to half an SD. But half an SD is
exactly Cohen's "medium" d = 0.5. A distribution-based MCID therefore adds
no clinical information beyond effect-size mode: it relabels the d = 0.5
boundary in clinical language. If no anchor-based MCID exists, saying so
and using `geom_es_zones()` is the more honest presentation.

## Within-patient MCIDs and between-group contrasts

Most MCIDs are defined for **change within a patient**: how much an
individual's score must move for that individual to notice. Contrasts from
a trial or an ANOVA are **differences between group means**. Reading a
between-group difference against a within-patient MCID is common, but
contested: a mean difference smaller than the MCID can arise when a
fraction of patients improve by much more than the MCID and the rest do not
change, and a mean difference larger than the MCID does not imply that
every patient improved by that much. The background shows where the
estimate lies relative to the threshold; it cannot tell you how individual
responses are distributed.

When you present group differences over MCID zones, say which kind of MCID
was used and where it comes from (`source`), and consider reporting
responder proportions alongside.

## Asymmetric and uncertain MCIDs

Thresholds for deterioration and improvement need not be equal, and the
literature often gives more than one estimate of an MCID. Both are
supported: `lower` and `upper` are set separately, and either can be a
range.

```{r asym}
thr <- mcid_thresholds(
  lower = -0.25,             # deterioration threshold
  upper = c(0.3, 0.5),       # improvement: two anchor studies disagree
  source = "Hypothetical anchors"
)
thr
plot_contrasts(TukeyHSD(fit), zones = geom_mcid_zones(thr, labels = TRUE))
```

A range is drawn as a fade from one zone into the next across the whole
range, so the reader sees where the threshold is uncertain instead of a
sharp line placed at an arbitrary point within it. Point thresholds have
hard edges unless you set `softness`.

With `beyond = "multiples"` the colour keeps deepening at 2× and 3× the
MCID, so an estimate just past the threshold and one far beyond it do not
share a background:

```{r multiples}
plot_contrasts(TukeyHSD(fit),
               zones = geom_mcid_zones(thr, beyond = "multiples"))
```

If lower values of the outcome are better (pain, symptom scores), set
`direction = "lower_better"` and the benefit and harm sides swap.

For black-and-white output use `palette = "grey"`. Grey levels have no
natural direction, so add `labels = TRUE` or keep the legend:

```{r grey}
plot_contrasts(TukeyHSD(fit),
               zones = geom_mcid_zones(thr, palette = "grey", labels = TRUE))
```

## Why the package does not classify results

It would be easy to add a function that reports, for each estimate, the
zone its point estimate falls in, or the probability that the true effect
is "beneficial", "trivial" or "harmful". effectzones deliberately does not.

That procedure is known as magnitude-based inference (Batterham & Hopkins
2006). Its classifications look like conclusions, but they interpret a
confidence interval as if it were a posterior distribution under an
implicit flat prior. Welsh & Knight (2015) showed that it is neither a
sound frequentist nor a coherent Bayesian procedure, and Sainani (2018)
showed that its type I error rates can be several times those of standard
hypothesis tests, depending on sample size and thresholds. A plotting package that printed such
labels would lend them authority they do not have.

The zones are a reading aid. The inference is the interval; the judgement
is yours, and it should be argued in the text, with the thresholds and
their source stated.
